Creating a thread here for the last remaining unknown implication for the finite graph, whether 677 x = y ◇ (x ◇ ((y ◇ x) ◇ y)) implies 255 x = ((x ◇ x) ◇ x) ◇ x.

We know remarkably little about this equation. @Pace Nielsen worked out that the solutions over a generic field to a linear model x⋄y=αx+βyx \diamond y = \alpha x + \beta yx⋄y=αx+βy come in two flavors. Type 1: β\betaβ is negative a primitive 5th root of unity (i.e. a root of x4+x3+x2+x1x^4+x^3+x^2+x^1x4+x3+x2+x1 and α=1−β\alpha = 1-\betaα=1−β (so it is a translation-invariant model). Type 2: β\betaβ is a root of x4+x3+2x2+2x+1x^4+x^3+2x^2+2x+1x4+x3+2x2+2x+1 and α=−β3−β−1\alpha=−\beta^3−\beta−1α=−β3−β−1, which (as observed by @Ben Gunby-Mann) also implies α2+α+1=0\alpha^2+\alpha+1=0α2+α+1=0 (i.e., α\alphaα is a primitive root of unity). Unfortunately, for such models 255 factors as (α2+α+1)(α+β−1)=0.(\alpha^2+\alpha+1)(\alpha+\beta−1)=0.(α2+α+1)(α+β−1)=0.

The smallest non-trivial model is of order 5; this particular example is x⋄y=2x−yx \diamond y = 2x - yx⋄y=2x−y on Z/5Z{\mathbb Z}/5{\mathbb Z}Z/5Z.

Empirically, the magma cohomology approach seems to fail for this equation, but we do not have a satisfactory explanation as to why.
So at least in the Type 1 models we'll have x2=xx^2 = xx2=x. So if I understand correctly that means that the implication is immune to linear models.

This 677->255 implication is immune to all linear models based on a (not necessarily commutative) ring where left-invertible ⇔ right-invertible (this includes finite rings and finite matrices over a field for instance).

The required equations to obey 677 are β(α+βαβ)=1\beta(\alpha+\beta\alpha\beta)=1β(α+βαβ)=1 and 0=α+β3+β2α20=\alpha+\beta^3+\beta^2\alpha^20=α+β3+β2α2. We want to show the condition for 255, which is (1+α+α2)(β+α−1)=0(1+\alpha+\alpha^2)(\beta+\alpha-1)=0(1+α+α2)(β+α−1)=0. To proceed, we work with β\betaβ and γ=α+β−1\gamma=\alpha+\beta-1γ=α+β−1. Note that the first assumption makes β\betaβ invertible. The two assumptions are

γβ+β−1γ=β2−β+1−β−1−β−2,γ2=(β−2−β−1−β−2)γ.\gamma\beta + \beta^{-1}\gamma = \beta^2 - \beta + 1 - \beta^{-1} - \beta^{-2} , \qquad \gamma^2 = (\beta-2-\beta^{-1}-\beta^{-2})\gamma .γβ+β−1γ=β2−β+1−β−1−β−2,γ2=(β−2−β−1−β−2)γ.

The first equation tells us how β\betaβ commutes through γ\gammaγ: intuitively it is mapped as β→−β−1\beta\to-\beta^{-1}β→−β−1. This is an involution, so we can get useful mileage from commuting through γ2\gamma^2γ2. Namely, we write β−1γ2β−γ2=[β−1γ,γβ+β−1γ]\beta^{-1}\gamma^2\beta-\gamma^2 = [\beta^{-1}\gamma, \gamma\beta+\beta^{-1}\gamma]β−1γ2β−γ2=[β−1γ,γβ+β−1γ] and compute the LHS using the formula for γ2\gamma^2γ2 and the RHS using the formula for γβ+β−1γ\gamma\beta+\beta^{-1}\gammaγβ+β−1γ. After reordering β,γ\beta,\gammaβ,γ using the first identity, we get a formula of the form f(β)γ=g(β)f(\beta)\gamma=g(\beta)f(β)γ=g(β). Right-multiplying by γ\gammaγ and reducing γ2\gamma^2γ2 we get h(β)γ=0h(\beta)\gamma=0h(β)γ=0. If I didn't mess up my calculations, we have enough to deduce (3−3β+β2+3γ−βγ−γβ+γ2)γ=0(3-3\beta+\beta^2+3\gamma-\beta\gamma-\gamma\beta+\gamma^2)\gamma=0(3−3β+β2+3γ−βγ−γβ+γ2)γ=0, which is 255.

I think I have also used Magma to rule out all non-commutative linear models modelled on a vector space with scalar field of characteristic 0 or positive characteristic less than 10000. In this online calculator one can run 

for p in PrimesUpTo(10000) do
    F<a, b, c> := FreeAlgebra(FiniteField(p),3);
    B := [(-1)+(b*a)+(b*b*a*b),(a)+(b*b*a*a)+(b*b*b),(b*b*a*c)+(b*b*c)+(b*c)+(c)];
    I := ideal<F | B>;
    if not ((-1)+(a*a*a)+(a*a*b)+(a*b)+(b) in I and (a*a*c)+(a*c)+(c) in I) then
        print(p);
    end if;
end for;
print("Done");

to test small characteristics. (And testing the rationals is similar).

When I worked out the two solutions over a generic field, I actually worked out the full reduction system over (potentially noncommutative) rings. For a map of the form x⋄y=ax+by+cx\diamond y=ax+by+cx⋄y=ax+by+c, a reduction system is given by

ba↦ab,b3↦a2b+b2+a2−a,a2b↦−a3−ab−b+1,ba\mapsto ab,\qquad b^3\mapsto a^2b+b^2+a^2-a,\qquad a^2b\mapsto -a^3-ab-b+1,ba↦ab,b3↦a2b+b2+a2−a,a2b↦−a3−ab−b+1,

a4↦ab2+2a3+ab−a2+b+a−2,b2ac↦−b2c−bc−c,a^4\mapsto ab^2+2a^3+ab-a^2+b+a-2,\qquad b^2ac\mapsto -b^2c-bc-c,a4↦ab2+2a3+ab−a2+b+a−2,b2ac↦−b2c−bc−c,

a2c↦−ac−c,b2c↦abc+aca^2c\mapsto -ac-c,\qquad b^2c\mapsto abc+aca2c↦−ac−c,b2c↦abc+ac

(255 does indeed follow for such linear maps over rings.)

A diagnosis of linear models is that all (finite) linear models are Latin squares (the condition b(a+bab)=1b(a+bab)=1b(a+bab)=1 makes bbb invertible, then the condition (1+b2a)a=−b3(1+b^2a)a=-b^3(1+b2a)a=−b3 makes aaa invertible). It's clear that 677 implies that left multiplication is invertible, since im(Ly)\text{im}(L_y)im(Ly​) is the whole magma and surjective implies injective. Both prover9 and mace4 are inconclusive on whether right multiplication has to be invertible in a general 677 magma (I am not very good with these tools though). This could influence the type of counterexamples we seek.

Terry used x⋄y=yx\diamond y=yx⋄y=y as a fall-back rule for his gigantic 1518 example because this was an easy way to fulfill the equation for most of the table. Here one option is to use a linear fallback, but the linear models are somewhat complicated. Another option is to use as a fallback a magma satisfying equation 14 (x=y⋄(x⋄y)x = y \diamond (x \diamond y)x=y⋄(x⋄y)), but modifying the squares (or the products involving squares). Then for most x,yx,yx,y the equation would reduce to x=y⋄x2x=y\diamond x^2x=y⋄x2. I didn't push this yet, in part because I wasn't sure if I had to make the magma right-cancellative.

Sorry, you're right, imposing equations 14 and 13 at the same time makes no sense. I had started an attempt by partitioning the magma in two subsets, but I don't have anything concrete at this stage.

The question of right-cancellation remains. In some sense, we need multiplication to preserve all the information in the right operand (due to left-cancellation) and at least "half" of the information in the left operand: indeed, the equation can be written as x=Lx′(Lx′′(y))x = L_{x'}(L_{x''}(y))x=Lx′​(Lx′′​(y)) where x′=y⋄xx' = y\diamond xx′=y⋄x and x′′=y⋄x′x''=y\diamond x'x′′=y⋄x′, and we want the pair of Lx′L_{x'}Lx′​ and Lx′′L_{x''}Lx′′​ to uniquely determine xxx (for a given yyy). So maybe a better starting point would be to try a carrier M=P×PM=P\times PM=P×P and (x1,x2)⋄(y1,y2)=f(x2,y1,y2)(x_1,x_2)\diamond(y_1,y_2) = f(x_2,y_1,y_2)(x1​,x2​)⋄(y1​,y2​)=f(x2​,y1​,y2​) to find an example of 677 magma that is not right-cancellative. If we impose bijectivity of left and right multiplications, then 677 implies 255. Here is a Prover9 proof (it only uses left injectivity and right surjectivity):

677 plus left multiplication bijective plus x^2 = y^2 implies 255.

I'm running a search of 677+left mult bijective + equation against 255, where equation ranges in [2,4694]. For now there are only 225 candidates left; I'll update soon.

The specific idea of dropping uniformly the "same half" of the left operand fails. In the equation written (in the finite case) as x = (y ◇ x) ◇ ((y ◇ (y ◇ x)) ◇ y), that would mean that the only dependence on y1 is from the last variable, and this dependence never disappears because this y is acted on by bijective L_{y ◇ x} and L_{y ◇ (y ◇ x)}. So we need more mixing.

So, that was a complete failure: mutation didn't work at all here, despite a fresh run.

I had one last faint hope that I simply had too few samples, but even after I had the dozens of linear models to play with thanks to Ibrahim, no luck. They're too tightly coupled together to use as good seeds. If you remove too few cells you wind up completing back to the original, and if you don't, you get an enormous number of linked failures which don't seem repairable. Reducing to a partial solution using fewer elements and trying to grow that, which helped before, also didn't work. Frankly, both vampire and mace4 have trouble finding the known solutions for me without a lot of prompting at larger N, although that might not apply to less coupled solutions, to be fair.

Efforts to use 614 as a base and then migrate back towards 677 didn't work either, and I can't even use the trick of driving toward a solution gradually by imposing some of an equation's implications because 677 doesn't have any in our set.

For evolutionary approaches to work, you need at least to be able to jump from one useful state (target or not) to another efficiently. This fails when useful states are too rare or it takes too long to get a new state, both of which seem to be true here.

Jose Brox said:

Bruno Le Floch ha dicho:

Both prover9 and mace4 are inconclusive on whether right multiplication has to be invertible in a general 677 magma (I am not very good with these tools though).

If we impose bijectivity of left and right multiplications, then 677 implies 255. Here is a Prover9 proof (it only uses left injectivity and right surjectivity):
PROVER9 677 plus left and right mult bijective implies 255 PROOF.txt

This feels like an important clue to me. For finite magmas we get left injectivity for free. If we can get a human proof of why right surjectivity implies 255 that should make it clearer what a counterexample might look like (or what a proof might look like - this implication could well be true for finite magmas!).

One possible thought is to try to adapt a technique that worked for weak central groupoids (see blueprint), which is to find a small (e.g., order 2) "relaxed" solution to 677 (where the magma operation is slightly multivalued), and try to build an extension of that by some pseudo-greedy algorithm. This amounts to imposing a coloring on the magma and imposing some rules about how the color of x⋄yx \diamond yx⋄y relates to the color of xxx and yyy (e.g., if xxx is red and yyy is blue, then x⋄yx \diamond yx⋄y must be blue, but if xxx and yyy are both red, then x⋄yx \diamond yx⋄y could be either red or blue, etc.). It may be possible to "decouple" the magma structure this way, for instance one could try to make the equation 13 hold for red elements and 14 hold for blue elements, thus dodging the issue that 13 and 14 are not compatible with each other. However I don't know if there is a practical relaxed magma that can be used as a base (of course one can always use the trivial relaxation in which every color output is permitted, but this doesn't gain anything).

There are no 677 models of size 2, 3, 4, and 6. I've been running a Vampire search for a model of order 8 for 26 hours but it still hasn't found one.

It's relatively rare for a two-variable equation such as 677 to have so few models, and so much restriction on the order. Weak central groupoids (1485) also had a lot of restrictions on the order, but that's a three-variable equation, so less surprising (it imposes n3n^3n3 constraints rather than n2n^2n2 constraints).

On the other hand, in contrast to say 854, 677 does not seem to be implying a lot of other laws (Equation Explorer only lists the trivial consequence 614, even if one assumes finiteness). So this equation is imposing some "rigidity", but the rigidity is coming from an unknown source.

This one is subtle: according to its manual, when parsing free variables in clauses and formulas Prover9 assumes they are universally quantified at the outermost level. I had understood this fact to be relative, i.e., to mean "at the outermost level of each subformula given by parentheses", but it is in fact absolute, meaning "at the outermost level of the global formula". Hence
x*y = x*z -> y = z works as intended, but
(x*y = x*z -> y = z)<->(all u all v exists w (w*u = v)) actually means
all x all y all z ((y*x = z*x -> y = z) <-> (all u all v exists w (w*u = v))) instead of
(all x all y all z (y*x = z*x -> y = z)) <-> (all u all v exists w (w*u = v)). The variant
all x all y all z (y*x = z*x -> y = z) <-> all u all v exists w (w*u = v) also works as intended.

So, using left cancellativity, one can describe the relation between ⋄\diamond⋄ and fff by two axioms:

  1. If y⋄x=zy \diamond x = zy⋄x=z, then z⋄y=f(x,y)z \diamond y = f(x,y)z⋄y=f(x,y).
  2. If y⋄z=xy \diamond z = xy⋄z=x, then x⋄f(x,y)=zx \diamond f(x,y) = zx⋄f(x,y)=z.

So I tried first choosing the function f:M×M→Mf: M \times M \to Mf:M×M→M, and seeing if one could build a magma operation ⋄\diamond⋄ that obeyed Axiom 1 and Axiom 2 for that choice of fff. The point is that the axioms are rather simple: both axioms assert that one entry in the multiplication table propagates to another. The problem is that these axioms don't commute, and in principle after N applications of these axioms, a single entry y⋄x=zy \diamond x = zy⋄x=z on the table can propagate into 2^N other entries, leading almost certainly to collisions. One somehow wants to choose an fff with a special property that the propagation rules of Axiom 1 and Axiom 2 (i.e., the functions (y,x,z)↦(z,y,f(x,y))(y,x,z) \mapsto (z,y,f(x,y))(y,x,z)↦(z,y,f(x,y)) and (y,z,x)↦(x,f(x,y),z)(y,z,x) \mapsto (x,f(x,y),z)(y,z,x)↦(x,f(x,y),z)) obey a lot of algebraic relations that cuts down on this complexity, but setting fff to be too simple (e.g., constant) quickly leads one to violate the requirement that each entry of the multiplication table has a unique answer. Hopefully, the answers will help refine the main axis of effort instead of just satisfying my personal curiosity.

  1. Do we know any finite models of 677 that are not outright cancellative? If not, do we have proof (or at least some heuristic) telling us not to expect such models?   2. Do we know any finite models of 677 that have even order? If not, do we have reason not to expect such models?
  3. Do we know two non-isomorphic finite models of 677 that have the same order? If not...
  4. How many different models do we know? How many models of order less than 15?

Perhaps the tools of classical universal algebra could help in such investigations? I mean things like subdirect representation, congruence lattices, characterizations of direct irreducibility.

Here's a concrete idea: If finite directly irreducible 677-magmas satisfy 255, then of course all finite 677-magmas do. Over certain algebraic structures, one can determine direct reducibility by counting solutions to equations. For example, a finite Heyting algebra is directly reducible precisely if the equation x∨¬x=⊤x \vee \neg x = \topx∨¬x=⊤ has more than 2 solutions (btw this is why all finite Boolean algebras have 2n2^n2n elements).

I wonder if 677-magmas admit any similar solution-counting characterization for direct reducibility. If so, these could be added as assumptions to Prover9 to see if they allow us to conclude e.g. right-cancellativity or 255.

I tested this on the extension models found by @Matthew Bolan here. All of them have idempotents (and sometimes every element is an idempotent). Some of them don't give a commutative auxiliary magma for any choice of idempotent, some give a commutative one for only a single choice of idempotent. But only three give an associative auxiliary magma: the first (index 0) magma (of order 25), and two magmas of order 121 (at indices 98 and 240). All three are idempotent, and any element works as the 0.

Note that a finite cancellative unital magma will have both left and right inverses because LxL_xLx​ and RxR_xRx​ are surjective. If the magma is commutative then they are equal by cancellativity, and if the magma is associative these inverses will be equal by the usual argument. So in fact all of the commutative auxiliary magmas have inverses including the three associative ones, so they are in fact abelian groups. And according to my calculations the functions are also homomorphisms, so these could be linear. I am not sure how to determine whether they admit a ring structure that makes the homomorphisms into left-multiplication operations.

One clear problem we have is the rigidity of 677: it doesn't imply many other identities, so it is satisfied by fewer models, hence the finite search against 255 is costly. Given an equation ppp, call a relaxation to any equation qqq such that p⇒qp\Rightarrow qp⇒q (call ppp a constriction of qqq). Obvious facts: A relaxation qqq of ppp has more models than ppp has, and qqq is a necessary condition for a model to satisfy ppp. If q⇒rq\Rightarrow rq⇒r then necessarily p⇒rp\Rightarrow rp⇒r. To show that p⇏rp\not\Rightarrow rp⇒r, it may be easier to start with a model of q⇏rq\not\Rightarrow rq⇒r and then modify such model to get the desired one.

Most relaxations may be trivial, at least to the human eye (i.e., substitutions), but perhaps we can find some interesting ones, or some easier for the ATPs to establish proofs with. With this in mind, I have tried to determine the relaxations of 677 up to 13*10^6. The (mostly raw) results follow:

I made a c++ program which outputs a DIMACS CNF format with O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) variables and O(n4)O(n^4)O(n4) clauses. This CNF will be satisfied if there is a magma which satisfies 677 but not 255 (If I haven't messed up).

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    using ssize_t = long long;

    if(argc != 2) {
        std::cerr << "Usage: " << argv[0] << " [Number of elements]" << std::endl;
        return 1;
    }

    ssize_t n;
    try {
        n = std::stoll(argv[1]);
        if(n < 0) { throw std::invalid_argument("Number of elements must be non-negative."); }
        if(n > 1'000'000) { throw std::invalid_argument("Number of elements is too large."); }
    } catch(std::exception const &e) {
        std::cerr << e.what() << std::endl;
        return 1;
    }

    std::vector<std::vector<ssize_t>> clauses;
    /** `var1(x, y, i)` is $X_{yx, i}$. */
    auto const var1 = [n](ssize_t const x, ssize_t const y, ssize_t const i) noexcept {
        return 1 + (x * n + y) * n + i;
    };
    /** `var2(x, y, i)` is $X_{(yx)y, i}$. */
    auto const var2 = [n](ssize_t const x, ssize_t const y, ssize_t const i) noexcept {
        return 1 + n * n * n + (x * n + y) * n + i;
    };
    /** `var3(x, y, i)` is $X_{x((yx)y), i}$. */
    auto const var3 = [n](ssize_t const x, ssize_t const y, ssize_t const i) noexcept {
        return 1 + 2 * n * n * n + (x * n + y) * n + i;
    };
    /** `var4(x, i)` is $X_{((xx)x)x, i}$. */
    auto const var4 = [n](ssize_t const x, ssize_t const i) noexcept {
        return 1 + 3 * n * n * n + x * n + i;
    };

    /** For every $x$ and $y$, exactly one of $X_{yx, i}$ for $0 \leq i < N$ is true. */
    for(ssize_t x = 0; x < n; x++) {
        for(ssize_t y = 0; y < n; y++) {
            /**
             * For each distinct pair $X_{yx, i}$ and $X_{yx, j}$ of variables,
             * there is at least one false variable. */
            for(ssize_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                for(ssize_t j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
                    clauses.push_back({-var1(x, y, i), -var1(x, y, j)});
                }
            }

            /** There is at least one true $X_{yx, i}$. */
            std::vector<ssize_t> clause;
            clause.reserve(n);
            for(ssize_t i = 0; i < n; i++) { clause.push_back(var1(x, y, i)); }
            clauses.push_back(std::move(clause));
        }
    }

    /** For every $x$ and $y$, exactly one of $X_{(yx)y, i}$ for $0 \leq i < n$ is true. */
    for(ssize_t x = 0; x < n; x++) {
        for(ssize_t y = 0; y < n; y++) {
            /**
             * For each distinct pair $X_{(yx)y, i}$ and $X_{(yx)y, j}$ of variables,
             * there is at least one false variable. */
            for(ssize_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                for(ssize_t j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
                    clauses.push_back({-var2(x, y, i), -var2(x, y, j)});
                }
            }

            /** There is at least one true $X_{(yx)y, i}$. */
            std::vector<ssize_t> clause;
            clause.reserve(n);
            for(ssize_t i = 0; i < n; i++) { clause.push_back(var2(x, y, i)); }
            clauses.push_back(std::move(clause));
        }
    }

    /**
     * For every $x$, $y$, and $i$, $X_{(yx)y, i}$ is true if and only if there is some $j$ which
     * $X_{yx, j}$ and $X_{jy, i}$ are true.
     *
     * As we assumed there exists a unique $i$ which makes $X_{yx, j}$ true, we may simplify the
     * proposition as follows.
     *
     * For every $x$, $y$, and $i$, $X_{(yx)y, i}$ is true if and only if for every $j$ which
     * $X_{yx, j}$ is true, $X_{jy, i}$ is also true. */
    for(ssize_t x = 0; x < n; x++) {
        for(ssize_t y = 0; y < n; y++) {
            for(ssize_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                for(ssize_t j = 0; j < n; j++) {
                    clauses.push_back({var1(y, j, i), -var1(x, y, j), -var2(x, y, i)});
                    clauses.push_back({var2(x, y, i), -var1(x, y, j), -var1(y, j, i)});
                }
            }
        }
    }

    /** For every $x$ and $y$, exactly one of $X_{x((yx)y), i}$ for $0 \leq i < n$ is true. */
    for(ssize_t x = 0; x < n; x++) {
        for(ssize_t y = 0; y < n; y++) {
            /**
             * For each distinct pair $X_{x((yx)y), i}$ and $X_{x((yx)y), j}$ of variables,
             * there is at least one false variable. */
            for(ssize_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                for(ssize_t j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
                    clauses.push_back({-var3(x, y, i), -var3(x, y, j)});
                }
            }

            /** There is at least one true $X_{x((yx)y), i}$. */
            std::vector<ssize_t> clause;
            clause.reserve(n);
            for(ssize_t i = 0; i < n; i++) { clause.push_back(var3(x, y, i)); }
            clauses.push_back(std::move(clause));
        }
    }

    /**
     * For every $x$, $y$, and $i$, $X_{x((yx)y), i}$ is true if and only if there is some $j$ which
     * $X_{(yx)y, j}$ and $X_{xj, i}$ are true.
     *
     * As we assumed there exists a unique $i$ which makes $X_{(yx)y, i}$ true, we may simplify the
     * proposition as follows.
     *
     * For every $x$, $y$, and $i$, $X_{x((yx)y), i}$ is true if and only if for every $j$ which
     * $X_{(yx)y, j}$ is true, $X_{xj, i}$ is also true. */
    for(ssize_t x = 0; x < n; x++) {
        for(ssize_t y = 0; y < n; y++) {
            for(ssize_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                for(ssize_t j = 0; j < n; j++) {
                    clauses.push_back({var1(j, x, i), -var2(x, y, j), -var3(x, y, i)});
                    clauses.push_back({var3(x, y, i), -var2(x, y, j), -var1(j, x, i)});
                }
            }
        }
    }

    /** For every $x$, $y$, and $i$, if $X_{x((yx)y), i}$ is true, then $X_{yi, x}$ is also true. */
    for(ssize_t x = 0; x < n; x++) {
        for(ssize_t y = 0; y < n; y++) {
            for(ssize_t i = 0; i < n; i++) { clauses.push_back({var1(i, y, x), -var3(x, y, i)}); }
        }
    }

    /** For every $x$, exactly one of $X_{((xx)x)x, i}$ for $0 \leq i < n$ is true. */
    for(ssize_t x = 0; x < n; x++) {
        /**
         * For each distinct pair $X_{((xx)x)x, i}$ and $X_{((xx)x)x, j}$ of variables,
         * there is at least one false variable. */
        for(ssize_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            for(ssize_t j = i + 1; j < n; j++) { clauses.push_back({-var4(x, i), -var4(x, j)}); }
        }

        /** There is at least one true $X_{((xx)x)x, i}$. */
        std::vector<ssize_t> clause;
        clause.reserve(n);
        for(ssize_t i = 0; i < n; i++) { clause.push_back(var4(x, i)); }
        clauses.push_back(std::move(clause));
    }

    /**
     * For every $x$ and $i$, $X_{((xx)x)x, i}$ is true if and only if there is some $j$ which
     * $X_{(xx)x, j}$ and $X_{jx, i}$ are true.
     *
     * As we assumed there exists a unique $i$ which makes $X_{(xx)x, i}$ true, we may simplify the
     * proposition as follows.
     *
     * For every $x$ and $i$, $X_{((xx)x)x, i}$ is true if and only if for every $j$ which
     * $X_{(xx)x, j}$ is true, $X_{jx, i}$ is also true. */
    for(ssize_t x = 0; x < n; x++) {
        for(ssize_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            for(ssize_t j = 0; j < n; j++) {
                clauses.push_back({var1(x, j, i), -var2(x, x, j), -var4(x, i)});
                clauses.push_back({var4(x, i), -var2(x, x, j), -var1(x, j, i)});
            }
        }
    }

    /**
     * We want to find a case when the equation 677 (x = y(x((yx)y))) is satisfied but the equation
     * 255 (x = ((xx)x)x) is not.
     *
     * If there is some $x$ which $X_{((xx)x)x, x}$ is false, then we are done. */
    {
        std::vector<ssize_t> clause;
        clause.reserve(n);
        for(ssize_t x = 0; x < n; x++) { clause.push_back(-var4(x, x)); }
        clauses.push_back(std::move(clause));
    }

    // DIMACS CNF Generation start
    std::cout << "p cnf " << 3 * n * n * n + n * n << ' ' << clauses.size() << '\n';
    for(auto const &clause: clauses) {
        for(auto const lit: clause) { std::cout << lit << ' '; }
        std::cout << "0\n";
    }
}

I was playing around with a graphical interpretation of (left-invertible) 677 and came up with the following, though I wasn't able to get further with it. We replace the magma operation with a labeled directed graph by writing x→yzx \stackrel{y}{\to} zx→yz if y⋄x=zy \diamond x = zy⋄x=z. Then left cancellability means that the edges labeled by yyy form a permutation. The law 677 then concerns paths of the form

a→eb→dc→ad→ae. a \stackrel{e}{\to} b \stackrel{d}{\to} c \stackrel{a}{\to} d \stackrel{a}{\to} e.a→eb→dc→ad→ae.

Namely, any incomplete path that contains all of the above four edges except for one of the first three, can be completed by adding in the missing edge. For instance,
a→eb→dc?d→ae a \stackrel{e}{\to} b \stackrel{d}{\to} c \quad ? \quad d \stackrel{a}{\to} ea→eb→dc?d→ae
can be completed to
a→eb→dc→ad→ae. a \stackrel{e}{\to} b \stackrel{d}{\to} c \stackrel{a}{\to} d \stackrel{a}{\to} e.a→eb→dc→ad→ae.
Indeed, if one replaces a,da, da,d by y,xy,xy,x and performs all the obvious substitutions, then the incomplete path is
y→y⋄x(y⋄x)⋄y→xx⋄((y⋄x)⋄y)?x→yy⋄x y \stackrel{y \diamond x}{\to} (y \diamond x) \diamond y \stackrel{x}{\to} x \diamond ((y \diamond x) \diamond y) \quad ? \quad x \stackrel{y}{\to} y \diamond xy→y⋄x(y⋄x)⋄y→xx⋄((y⋄x)⋄y)?x→yy⋄x
and completing the path precisely corresponds to 677 holding for this choice of x,yx,yx,y. Completing the first or second edge corresponds to other equivalent forms of 677 (assuming left cancellativity) that we have worked out in the past (and are also recorded in the blueprint). (Completing the final edge is more problematic, this seems to require right cancellativity which we know can fail.)

As Vlad Tsyrklevich points out, one reason comes by an argument from ignorance: assuming something fails because we tried hard but failed to prove that it holds. Indeed, we tried all our tricks to prove the 677->255 implication but made no progress. If it holds, its proof has to be quite unlike any other proof we've done over the course of the project.

But that's not all. As things stand, it looks quite plausible to me that most non-right-cancellative models of 677 would refute 677->255, and we're just not very good at constructing such models. Let me elaborate.

We know that a countermodel to 677 -> 255 cannot be right-cancellative. Constructing a non-right-cancellative model of 677 is therefore no harder than constructing a countermodel to 677->255. But when we actually try to construct non-right-cancellative finite models of 677, the very same difficulties appear as when we try to prove the 677->255 implication:

  1. Typical finiteness assumptions, such as function periodicity, injections coinciding with bijections, do not help our ATP tools prove the statement.
  2. Mace4 and similar tools fail to construct a countermodel, possibly because even the smallest ones exceed feasible size limits.
  3. The methods that we devised to extend existing models to larger models while refuting some property provably break down (i.e. we can prove that they would only work if the existing model was already a counterexample, and then there'd be no reason to use them).

Yet non-right-cancellative models of 677 turn out to exist! No small examples are known, of course: computer searches found none, and the smallest known case (whose table was computed by Matthew Bolan) has order 496. Worse, the only method we currently know to construct such models (due to Tao) always yields idempotent magmas, and such magmas cannot serve as counterexamples to 677->255.

The overall pattern, and the fact that we could eventually construct non-right-cancellative models of 677, strongly suggest to me that we will eventually be able to construct countermodels to 677->255 as well: all known difficulties appear quite similar. Indeed, it looks plausible to me that most non-right-cancellative models of 677 would refute 677->255 as well, and we just got unlucky in that the first working attempt to produce non-right-cancellative models yielded idempotent ones.

# Global variable to store the magma table
magma = []
n = 0

def load_file():
    global magma, n
    file_path = filedialog.askopenfilename(
        title="Select a magma file",
        filetypes=[("Text Files", "*.txt"), ("All Files", "*.*")]
    )
    if not file_path:
        return

    try:
        with open(file_path, "r") as f:
            lines = f.readlines()
        # First line gives n
        n = int(lines[0].strip())
        magma = []
        # Next n lines, each with n integers
        for i in range(1, n+1):
            row = list(map(int, lines[i].split()))
            if len(row) != n:
                raise ValueError("Row length does not match n")
            magma.append(row)
        messagebox.showinfo("Success", f"Loaded magma of size {n}.")
        update_dropdown()
    except Exception as e:
        messagebox.showerror("Error", f"Failed to load file: {e}")

def update_dropdown():
    # Update the dropdown list with numbers 0 to n-1.
    selector['menu'].delete(0, 'end')
    for i in range(n):
        selector['menu'].add_command(label=str(i), command=tk._setit(selected_number, str(i)))
    selected_number.set("0")

def draw_graph():
    if not magma:
        messagebox.showerror("Error", "No magma loaded!")
        return

    try:
        a = int(selected_number.get())
    except ValueError:
        messagebox.showerror("Error", "Invalid number selected!")
        return

    G = nx.DiGraph()
    # Add nodes labeled from 0 to n-1
    G.add_nodes_from(range(n))

    # For each b in 0..n-1, determine c = a * b and add a red edge (left multiplication)
    for b in range(n):
        c_left = magma[a][b]
        G.add_edge(b, c_left, color='red', label='L')

    # For each b in 0..n-1, determine c = b * a and add a blue edge (right multiplication)
    for b in range(n):
        c_right = magma[b][a]
        G.add_edge(b, c_right, color='blue', label='R')

    # Draw the graph using different colors for the two kinds of arrows
    pos = nx.spring_layout(G)  # Compute layout
    # Extract edge colors based on edge attributes
    edge_colors = [G[u][v]['color'] for u,v in G.edges()]

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    nx.draw(G, pos, with_labels=True, node_color='lightgreen', arrows=True, edge_color=edge_colors,
            connectionstyle='arc3, rad=0.1', node_size=800)

    # Optionally, you can add labels to edges if desired.
    # edge_labels = {(u, v): G[u][v]['label'] for u,v in G.edges()}
    # nx.draw_networkx_edge_labels(G, pos, edge_labels=edge_labels)

    plt.title(f"Graph for chosen element {a}")
    plt.show()

# Create the main window
root = tk.Tk()
root.title("Magma Graphical Helper")

# Button to load the file
load_button = tk.Button(root, text="Load Magma File", command=load_file)
load_button.pack(pady=10)

# Dropdown to choose an element from 0 to n-1
selected_number = tk.StringVar(root)
selected_number.set("Select element")
selector = tk.OptionMenu(root, selected_number, ())
selector.pack(pady=10)

# Button to draw the graph for the chosen number
draw_button = tk.Button(root, text="Draw Graph", command=draw_graph)
draw_button.pack(pady=10)

root.mainloop()

There is a lot of theory to be developed around Lie magmas, I don't want to get carried away too much in this thread, so I'll try to keep it short. For me, Lie magmas over R or C are real/complex manifolds equipped with a smooth (analytic?) binary operation, possibly obeying one of our equational laws. For instance Lie groups are equipped with g⋄h=gh−1g\diamond h=gh^{-1}g⋄h=gh−1 obeying the Higman-Neumann axiom.

Let me assume there is an idempotent (e.g. the identity element in a Lie group), and Taylor expand the magma operation in some coordinate patch around that idempotent point. Terms in the series are binary operations that are polynomial in a pair of tangent vectors. Only some combinations of them are coordinate-invariant (details have to do with magma cohomology). The first-order term in the Taylor series is a binary operation that is linear in its arguments and obeys whatever equational law we want to impose. E.g., for Lie groups (1+x)⋄(1+y)=1+(x−y)+…(1+x)\diamond(1+y)=1+(x-y)+\dots(1+x)⋄(1+y)=1+(x−y)+… thus this operation is subtraction, which is the only linear model obeying Higman-Neumann.

The Lie bracket can be found at quadratic order in two ways: as whatever remains after fixing coordinate invariance, or as a coordinate-invariant combination of the group operations. Let's work in G=GL(n,R)G=GL(n,\mathbb{R})G=GL(n,R) for concreteness, so x,yx,yx,y are n×nn\times nn×n matrices. (1) We have $(1+x)\diamond(1+y)=1+(x-y)+(-xy+y^2)+\dots$$. A coordinate redefinition changes x→x+B(x)+…x\to x+B(x)+\dotsx→x+B(x)+… and likewise for yyy and x−yx-yx−y with the same quadratic BBB, which changes the quadratic term to −xy+y2+B(x)−B(y)−B(x−y)=−xy+y2+2B(x,y)−2B(y)-xy+y^2+B(x)-B(y)-B(x-y) = -xy+y^2+2B(x,y)-2B(y)−xy+y2+B(x)−B(y)−B(x−y)=−xy+y2+2B(x,y)−2B(y) with B(x,y)B(x,y)B(x,y) being the corresponding symmetric bilinear form. Picking B(y)=y2/2B(y)=y^2/2B(y)=y2/2 we obtain −xy+(xy+yx)/2-xy+(xy+yx)/2−xy+(xy+yx)/2, which features the Lie bracket. (2) We have the usual way to get the Lie bracket from (1+x)⋄((1+y)⋄((1+y)⋄(1+x)))=(1+x)(1+y)(1+x)−1(1+y)−1=1+(yx−xy)+…(1+x)\diamond((1+y)\diamond((1+y)\diamond(1+x))) = (1+x)(1+y)(1+x)^{-1}(1+y)^{-1} = 1+(yx-xy)+…(1+x)⋄((1+y)⋄((1+y)⋄(1+x)))=(1+x)(1+y)(1+x)−1(1+y)−1=1+(yx−xy)+…. This combination of operations can probably be seen from magma cohomology.

For two-variable equations, the quadratic terms are not enough to fix higher-order terms. For three-variable equations I think they are often enough to fix all higher-order terms. However, even if the series converges the chart does not necessarily cover the whole Lie magma (for Lie central groupoids, I found a case where the law is obeyed as long as we stay in some patch but it doesn't seem possible to extend to a whole magma). For Lie groups, Lie's third theorem tells us it works, but its proofs are not very nice.

My hope is that some of that discussion also works over a finite field.

In fact, it can't be alternative on either side (that is, equations 4396 and 4473), or many combinations of these identities:
1. z * (x * (z * y)) = ((z * x) * z) * y
2. x * (z * (y * z)) = ((z * x) * z) * y

I had some fun building a custom DPLL-based model searcher entirely for equation 677 ^^
It's implemented here: https://github.com/memoryleak47/eq677/tree/main/src/c_dpll

The biggest perf effects were:

  • simple freshness: I toyed around with more complicated notions of symmetry-breaking eg. starting to guess the first row, but simple freshness worked the best so far. Simple freshness just means "If for both x and y, you know no equations (i.e. f(x, _) = _, or f(_, x) = _, or f(_, _) = x"), then x and y are indistinguishable, and it suffices to only consider x"
  • note that cadical is SAT-based, which this tool isn't. It's using constraints based on term equations x = f(y, f(x, f(f(y, x), y))) added for each pair of x, y. These constraints then simplify over time when more elements in the magma-matrix are filled out (using a listener scheme inspired by typical SAT watchers). This should generate far less constraints than you'd need in SAT, but I might miss some tricks there.
  • model splitting: initially branch on forall x: x*x = x, which if true, fills out the whole diagonal, and otherwise gives you some non-idempotent element x, which you can choose as element 0 (which allows you to assume 0*0 = 1). And simply assuming 0*0 = 1 makes the the tool quite a bit faster. You can observe the same with mace4.
  • When a constraint simplifies to x = f(a, f(b, c)) check whether we know some d with f(a, d) = x. if yes, we can prove f(b, c) = d.

Yes, 2-transitive examples have to be idempotent, so they cannot be minimal counterexamples of E677⊨E255. That said, it is not too difficult to enumerate them with GAP. Here is a a snippet:

GAP Snippet

TestE677 := function (m)
    local i,j;
    for i in [1..Length(m)] do
        for j in [1..Length(m)] do
            if (m[i][m[j][m[m[i][j]][i]]] <> j) then
                return false;
            fi;
        od;
    od;
    return true;
end;

FillMatrix := function (d,T,k)
    local m, i, g;
    m := NullMat(d,d);
    for i in [1..d] do
        m[i][i] := i;
    od;
    for g in T do
        m[1^g][2^g] := k^g;
    od;
    return m;
end;

ProduceExamples := function (n)
    local result, G, k, m, H, mp, T;
    Print(n, ":\n");
    result := [];
    for G in AllPrimitiveGroups(NrMovedPoints,[n],Transitivity,[2]) do
        Print(G, "\n");
        H := Stabiliser(Stabilizer(G,1),2);
        mp := MovedPoints(H);
        T := RightTransversal(G,H);
        for k in [1..n] do
            if (k in mp) then
                continue;
            fi;
            m := FillMatrix(n,T,k);
            if (TestE677(m)) then
                AddSet(result, m);
            fi;
        od;
    od;
    Print(result, "\n");
end;

Hey, new construction to combine models together:
Let ML be an idempotent magma whose computation of f(y, f(x, f(f(y, x), y))) never evaluates f(a, a) for any a, except if x=y held initially.

Let MR and MR' be two 677 models of the same size n.

Then you can build an extension of ML by

f((x, s), (y, t)) =
  if x=y: (ML(x, y), MR(s, t))
  else: (ML(x, y), MR'(s, t))

found 26 new models under size 100: https://github.com/memoryleak47/eq677/commit/883ca99e96ac2ba788bee48e3e48061d95b6b9da

Edit: And just like with gluing, by shuffling MR or MR', you can create many more non-isomorphic magmas from the same input magmas.

It won't directly help with 255 though, the magma generated by a single element will always be isomorphic to the magma generated by the corresponding element in MR.

Edit 2: An extended construction would choose MR depending on the value of x=y. So MR' would be for the case where x != y, and for each x=y one could provide a specialized MR_x.

Edit 3: This can be generalized further: We can group pairs of ML-elements (a, b) and (x, y) into equivalence classes, based on whether the evaluation of 677 (i.e. f(x, f(y, f(f(x, y), x)))) might depend on f(a, b). Any equivalence class of pairs {(a, b), (x, y) , ...} of elements in ML can get their corresponding MR_(a,b) magma.
Computationally, we start by having all pairs (x, y) as separate singleton equivalence classes, and then if while evaluating f(x, f(y, f(f(x, y), x))) we encounter f(a, b), we'd have to merge the classes of (a, b) and (x, y).

For this generalization ML doesn't need to be idempotent, but in order to be interesting it needs to have more than just one equivalence class.

Maybe there is a way to find a 677 -/> 255 counter example using this. If we find an element x in ML, s.t. during evaluation of 255 (i.e. in f(f(f(x, x), x), x)) it evaluates f(a, b) and f(c, d), where the pairs (a, b) and (c, d) are not in the same 677-equivalence-class, then we would be free to choose some MR_(a,b) and MR_(c,d) that makes 255 false. So far it looks however, as if the equivalence relation of 255 refines the equivalence relation of 677.

I was looking into a slightly different notion of equivalence classes, that might yield something useful:

Consider a coloring of pairs (x, y), s.t. if (x, y) and (a, b) agree in color, then their 677 traces (i.e. the sequence of pairs evaluated in their 677 computation) fully agree in color.

The motivating example is translation invariance, where the color is the value of y-x; if you know y-x, then you'll know the deltas of all further 677 computation steps in f(y, f(x, f(f(y, x), y)))

Now, if you look at 5/0, 11/0 or 11/1 minus idempotents, all of them have a 2-coloring:
For 5/0, if y-x is 2 or 3, it's red; and if it's 1 or 4 it's blue.

The traces of these colors yield:
red trace: [red, red, blue, red]
blue trace: [blue, blue, red, blue]

Which means that you can build an extension of 5/0, one for the blue and one for the red case.

f((x, s), (y, t)) = (M5(x, y), red(x, y)? f1(s, t): f2(s, t))

Using this we can rephrase 677 as:
x = f1(y, f2(x, f1(f1(y, x), y)))
x = f2(y, f1(x, f2(f2(y, x), y)))

x = f2(y, f2(x, f1(f1(y, x), y)))
x = f1(y, f1(x, f2(f2(y, x), y)))

We've been exploring Problem 8.1 (does E677 imply E255 for finite magmas?) from a computational and formal angle, mostly with Claude as a collaborator. We're not sure how much of this is already known or useful to anyone, so we're just posting everything we found. We're considering a PR to the ETP repo with some Lean files but would appreciate guidance on what's actually relevant.

Quick context: we started from the blueprint's Chapter 13 (Lemma 13.1/13.2, linear obstruction, free magma construction) and tried to push further both computationally and formally.

What we have in Lean 4 (Lean 4 Mathlib, ~480 lines across 3 files):

27 proven lemmas in the main file covering E614 derivation, L_y bijectivity, left cancellation, backward recurrence, fixer uniqueness, orbit recurrence, a σ² identity, a key identity relating (y ◇ (y ◇ x)) ◇ y to x ◇ (((y ◇ x) ◇ x) ◇ (y ◇ x)), a star equation (if a ◇ x = b ◇ x then the next-level products agree), and several E255 equivalences from Blueprint Lemma 13.2.

6 proven lemmas (0 sorry) for a translation-invariant reduction: if x ◇ y = x * f(x⁻¹ * y) on a group, then E255 reduces to a single equation f(γ⁻¹) = γ⁻¹ where γ = f(1) * f(f(1)⁻¹). The master equation (★) at a=1 gives f²(γ) = 1. The gap is that these are conditions on different elements (γ vs γ⁻¹) connected only through group inverse, which has no relationship to f.

3 sorry blocks: R_x injective on L_x-orbit (the main barrier), a bridge identity d₃ = e₄, and the main theorem.

Computational results (verified exhaustively on all 437 known finite E677 models from the eq677 database, sizes up to 496):

  1. Squaring identity equivalence: E255 at x is equivalent to c_{d-4} ◇ c_{d-4} = c_{d-5} (where c_k = L_x^k(x), d = orbit period). Proof uses orbit recurrence two applications of left cancellation each way. Verified on 16280 elements. We didn't see this in the blueprint but it might be known.

  2. Orbit injectivity is the barrier: the d-sequence d_k = L_x^k(x) ◇ x is injective on Z/dZ (26668/26668 elements, 0 failures). This is specific to the self-referential case; it fails for arbitrary (w, x) pairs. Every algebraic manipulation we tried (E677 left cancellation backward recurrence σ²) reduces proving this to right cancellation. We think the proof must use finiteness beyond orbit periodicity.

  3. Untwisting is impossible: we tested whether L_y⁻¹ could be expressed as R_z for some z depending only on y (the way E680's proof works). Result: 0/27164 (model, y) pairs. σ(x,y) = (y ◇ x) ◇ y always depends on x. Minimum Hamming distance from nearest R_z is 0.8n. The E680-style proof is definitively inapplicable.

  4. Bridge identity d₃ = e₄: the e-sequence e_k = L_{c₁}^k(x) provides a second coordinate system. d₃ = e₄ holds universally (0 failures) but is not an equational consequence of E677 (Prover9 confirms sos_empty).

  5. Orbit size constraints: d ∈ {1} ∪ {≥6}. Sizes 2,3,4,5 never occur. For d = 7 (most common): 86.8% of elements have affine orbit structure c_i ◇ c_j = c_{(4i j 1) mod 7}.

  6. SAT search on translation-invariant models, sizes 2 through 42: UNSAT (no counterexample).

  7. 13 novel depth-5 identities of the form T(x) = x that hold in all finite models but aren't equational consequences of E677. Haven't finished analyzing their algebraic content.

The overall picture from our end: every algebraic reformulation of E255 we found (fixer existence, squaring identity, orbit injectivity, TI fixed point, counting) is provably equivalent to E255. The proof seems to need a genuinely non-algebraic ingredient, probably counting/combinatorics via Fintype/Finset.

To answer your main question directly: No, I don't have a purely equational
path. The derivation relies on finiteness in two essential places:

1. L_y bijectivity — surjection on a finite set gives bijection, which gives a
clean inverse: L_y⁻¹(x) = x ◇ ((y◇x)◇y)

2. Orbit periodicity — L_x iterates cycle with some period p on a finite set,
so L_x⁻²(x) = x_{p-2} in the orbit

The Prover9 timeout at 120s is consistent with this — the identity is
genuinely finite-only, and I wouldn't expect an equational derivation to exist
given that E677 ⊭ E255 holds in the infinite case (greedy construction).

One reduction you may not have: The entire problem collapses to a single
injectivity question. Define θ(z) = (z◇z)◇z. Then:

- E255 holds at x ⟺ ∃y, y◇x = x
- The unique such y (by fixer-uniqueness) is y = θ(x)
- So E255 for all x ⟺ the map x ↦ "left identity of x" is total ⟺ θ is
surjective

- On a finite set, surjective ⟺ injective

So: E677 ⊨_fin E255 ⟺ θ is injective in every finite E677-magma. And θ(z) =
L_z⁻²(z), so this becomes: does z ◇ (z ◇ a) = z have at most one solution in
z, for each fixed a?

Verified computationally — θ is injective across all known finite E677 models
including the 496-element non-right-cancellative construction from the
blueprint.

 For a non-idempotent element x with left-orbit period p ≥ 5, define
 c_k = L_x^k(x). Then:

     E255 at x  ⟺  c_{p-4} ◇ c_{p-4} = c_{p-5}

 element five steps from the end. One self-squaring identity, at one

   which follows from the squaring permutation c_k ↦ c_{(1-2k) mod 7}.

Following up on the single-point reduction (https://zenodo.org/records/20047800), here are new structural findings from systematic computational analysis across 500+ models (sizes 5, 7, 31, 35, 496).

 1. L_x ∘ R_x has exactly one fixed point — universally

 The blueprint equivalence says E255 at x ⟺ ∃z: L_x(R_x(z)) = z. We verified computationally that L_x ∘ R_x has *exactly one* fixed point for *every* x in *every* tested model. This includes the 496-element blueprint construction where R_x is
 non-bijective (|image(R_x)| = 271/496).

 The uniqueness is provable: if z is a fixed point, then z◇x is a left-fixer of z, which is uniquely θ(z) by Lemma 677-Basic. So the fixed point, if it exists, is unique. The existence is the open problem.

 | Model | n | R_x bij | L_x∘R_x FP = 1 | FP = c_{p-3} |
 |-------|---|---------|-----------------|--------------|
 | All size-5 (6 models) | 5 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
 | All size-7 (500 models) | 7 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
 | Jihoon (5x+27y+1)%31 | 31 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
 | Adam's n=35 | 35 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
 | Blueprint 496 | 496 | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ |

 3500+ elements tested, zero exceptions.

 2. The fixed point is always c_{p-3}

 The unique fixed point of L_x ∘ R_x is always the orbit element c_{p-3} = L_x^{p-3}(x). The fixed-point condition at z = c_{p-3} gives:

     R_x(c_{p-3}) = L_x^{-1}(c_{p-3}) = c_{p-4}

 which is d_{p-3} = c_{p-4} — precisely the single-point identity from our preprint. So the abstract fixed-point question and the concrete orbit recurrence are the same problem, viewed from different angles.

 3. The d_k escape pattern: four universal anchors

 The sequence d_k = c_k ◇ x records R_x on the orbit. It does NOT always stay in the orbit:

 - Period 7 (size 7, 35): all d_k in orbit (orbit = whole magma or sub-magma)
 - Period 6 (size 7): d_k escapes at k=2 (540/540 orbits, zero exceptions)
 - Period 10 (Jihoon model): only 4 out of 10 d_k values are in-orbit

 But four positions are *always* in-orbit, universally:

 - d_0 = c_1 (provable)
 - d_1 = c_{p-2} (provable)
 - d_{p-3} = c_{p-4} (≡ single-point identity — TARGET)
 - d_{p-2} = c_0 = x (≡ E255 — TARGET)

 The first two are theorems. The last two are the goal. Intermediate d_k values escape the orbit freely.

 4. The R_x bottleneck — sharpest characterization of the difficulty

 E677 constraint propagation within the orbit multiplication table deadlocks completely. Starting from 12 provably known entries (orbit definition + d_0 + d_1), applying E677 as a rewrite rule produces zero new entries. The target T[p-4][p-4] =
 p-5 requires at least one additional R_x value on the orbit, which the orbit structure alone cannot provide.

 Furthermore, image(R_x) is NOT L_x-invariant in general (tested on 496-model: each L_x-orbit of size 30 has exactly 15/30 elements in image(R_x)).

 The core obstruction: L_x is fully understood (bijection, cyclic on orbit). R_x is the mystery. The proof must bring in information about R_x from outside the orbit — either a global property of R_x, cross-orbit E677 applications, or a counting
 argument.

 5. Boundary value problem reframing

 The d_k recurrence d_{k+1} = L_{c_k}^{-1}(c_{k-1}) is fully deterministic — each step applies a bijection of all of M, not just the orbit. The sequence starts from known values (d_0 = c_1, d_1 = c_{p-2}), passes through M freely, and must arrive
  at d_{p-3} = c_{p-4} after p-3 steps. This is a boundary value problem on a deterministic recurrence over a finite set.

 The finiteness is used essentially: in the free (infinite) E677 magma, the d_k sequence escapes immediately and never returns, because term trees grow monotonically. Orbit closure (finiteness) prevents this.

 Remaining approaches that address R_x directly:

 1. R_x image counting: Can finiteness + E677 force R_x to map at least one orbit element beyond the two known anchors back into the orbit at the right position?

 2. Left-fixer counting: Every L_y has at most one fixed point. The total Σ|Fix(L_y)| = |M| in all tested models. Can a double-counting argument on the fixer relation F = {(z,y) : y◇z = z} establish |F| = |M|?

 3. Minimal criminal: Smallest counterexample has |M| ≥ 7, non-idempotent elements, period p ≥ 5. At size 35, every non-idempotent orbit generates a size-7 sub-magma — can quotient arguments exploit this?

 Updated preprint forthcoming on Zenodo. Scripts at https://github.com/hawkaiglai/equational_theories.

 Any thoughts on the R_x bottleneck — especially whether the boundary value problem framing suggests proof techniques from dynamics or combinatorics?

What we have, clearly stated:

The question is whether E677 implies E255 for finite magmas. We have computational evidence (SAT solver) that the answer is yes, and a partial proof that decomposes the problem into two steps:

Step 1 (open): In a finite E677-magma, if x is non-idempotent, then right multiplication R_x is a bijection. This is SAT-verified through orbit period 10 but we have no algebraic proof.

Step 2 (proven for small cases, p ≤ 7): If the magma is additionally a quasigroup (R_x bijective for all x), then E255 holds. Here's the proof at period 5:

- Apply E677 at (x, x). Using L_x = orbit shift, this forces c_1 ◇ x = c_{p-2}. (Direct computation: the equation becomes (c_1 ◇ x + 2) mod p = 0.)
- Blueprint Lemma 13.1(iii) applied at (c_j, x) gives: c_{j+1} ◇ (c_{j+2} ◇ x) = c_j for all j.
- Since R_x is bijective, the column (c_0 ◇ x, c_1 ◇ x, ..., c_{p-1} ◇ x) is a permutation.

Sub-magma structure and a minimal criminal observation

I ran sub-magma analysis on the known models. Here's what I found:

Size 7 (50 magmas enumerated via Z3): Zero proper sub-magmas in any of them. Every non-idempotent element generates the entire magma under ◇. All 300 non-idempotent orbits generate M.

Adam's size-35 model: Decomposes into 5 copies of a size-7 E677 sub-magma (each non-idempotent orbit of size 7 is closed under ◇ and satisfies E677), plus idempotent elements.

Jihoon's size-31 model: No proper sub-magma found. Every orbit generates all of M.

This matters for the E255 question because of the following minimal criminal argument:

Suppose M is a smallest finite E677 magma where E255 fails at some element x. Then:

  1. |M| ≥ 7 (sizes ≤ 6 exhausted).
  2. M has no proper E677 sub-magma. (If it did, restrict to the sub-magma — it's a smaller E677 magma. If E255 fails there, it contradicts minimality. If E255 holds there, we have a sub-magma satisfying E255 — but then by Lemma 13.4, extensions of E255-satisfying sub-magmas also satisfy E255, giving a contradiction.)
  3. In particular, M cannot be a direct product of two smaller E677 magmas.

Now, Bernhard pointed out that R_x bijectivity fails in product constructions (non-idempotent model × non-right-cancellative model). But both factors are E677 sub-magmas, so this can't happen in a minimal criminal. This suggests:

Question: In a simple finite E677 magma (no proper E677 sub-magma), is R_x necessarily bijective for non-idempotent x?

If yes, the proof decomposes cleanly:

  • Step 0: Idempotent x → E255 trivially.
  • Step 1: Minimal criminal is simple → R_x bijective for non-idempotent x.
  • Step 2: E677 + R_x bijective → E255 (this is closely related to Lemma 13.2; SAT-verified through orbit period 30).

The computational evidence: R_x is bijective for every non-idempotent element in every simple E677 magma I've tested (all size-7 models, Jihoon's size-31).

Caveat about point 2 above: I'm applying Lemma 13.4 somewhat loosely. Lemma 13.4 covers linear extensions specifically (M = N × A with the product operation having a specific linear form). A general E677 sub-magma might not fit the hypotheses of 13.4. So the argument in point 2 needs checking: does E255 on a sub-magma always propagate to the full magma, or only for specific extension types?

If Lemma 13.4 doesn't cover all sub-magma extensions, the minimal criminal might have a proper sub-magma where E255 holds but the extension still fails E255. In that case, point 2 only says the sub-magma itself can't be a counterexample — the failure would come from elements outside the sub-magma.

I'd appreciate thoughts on whether this line of reasoning is sound, especially whether E255 propagation from sub-magmas to extensions holds more generally than Lemma 13.4 states.

In earlier posts I reported that "E677 + orbit=M + NOT E255" is UNSAT for p = 5 through 10 (and p ≤ 30 with a quasigroup assumption). I now realize these results are vacuous — they say nothing about E255.

The issue. The encoding fixes element 0 to have an L_0-orbit spanning the entire magma (i.e., L_0 is a single p-cycle). A follow-up existence check shows that no E677 magma with this property exists for any p except p = 7:
| p | E677 + (L_0 is a p-cycle), no E255 constraint | |---|---|
| 3–6 | UNSAT |
| 7| SAT (unique solution: the affine magma) |
| 8–10 | UNSAT |
Since the base system (E677 + orbit structure) is already contradictory for p ≠ 7, adding "NOT E255" changes
nothing — the solver proves UNSAT for reasons unrelated to E255. Only p = 7 has a satisfying assignment, and that unique magma happens to satisfy E255, but this is just one magma, not a general proof.
The quasigroup speedup I reported (3900× at p = 10) is similarly affected: it operates within the same vacuous setting.
I apologize for the confusion. The UNSAT cores I extracted from these encodings reflect the non-existence of the orbit structure, not the forcing of E255.
What does work: full-magma SAT (no orbit assumption)
Using a straightforward encoding — n² cells as variables, E677 imposed for all n² pairs (a, b), rows constrained to be permutations (since L_y is bijective in any finite E677 magma) — I confirmed:

  1. n = 5: E677 ∧ ¬E255 is UNSAT (CaDiCaL, 0.04s)
  2. n = 7: E677 ∧ ¬E255 is UNSAT (CaDiCaL, 78s)

    These are genuine proofs that every E677 magma of size 5 (respectively 7) satisfies E255. No orbit assumption, no quasigroup assumption. This extends to n ≤ 11 via Rudi's enumeration and Bernardo's faster encoding.
    Limitation: UNSAT core extraction from this encoding is currently intractable at n = 7 (the gated version needed for assumption-based cores doesn't finish within 10 minutes). So I have a proof exists but cannot yet inspect its structure.

I've posted an updated version of the paper on this problem:

https://zenodo.org/records/20257475

Below is a summary of what the paper contains.

Definitions (for reference)

We work in a finite magma $(M, \diamond)$ — a set with a binary operation, no other axioms assumed. The identities under study are:

  1. E677: $a = b \diamond (a \diamond ((b \diamond a) \diamond b))$ for all $a, b$
  2. 255: $((x \diamond x) \diamond x) \diamond x = x$ for all $x$

The question is whether E677 finitely entails E255 (written E677 $\models_\text{fin}$ E255), meaning: does every finite E677 magma satisfy E255? In infinite magmas this is false (greedy counterexample exists), so finiteness is essential.

Key maps: $L_y(z) = y \diamond z$ (left multiplication), $R_x(y) = y \diamond x$ (right multiplication), $S(x) = x \diamond x$ (squaring). E677 forces every $L_y$ to be bijective on a finite set.

For fixed $x$, the left orbit is $c_0 = x, \; c_1 = x \diamond x, \; c_k = L_x^k(x)$ with period $p$ (smallest $p \geq 1$ with $c_p = c_0$).

The theta map is $\theta(x) = (x \diamond x) \diamond x = c_1 \diamond x$. A left-fixer of $z$ is an element $w$ with $w \diamond z = z$; E677 forces left-fixers, when they exist, to be unique and equal to $\theta(z)$. E255 at $x$ is equivalent to: $\theta(x)$ is a left-fixer of $x$.

Results proved in the paper

  1. Periods 2 and 3 are impossible (Theorems 4.2, 4.3).

Complete algebraic proofs, no SAT needed.

  • Period 2: Assuming $x$ has orbit $\{x, c_1\}$ with $c_1 \diamond x = x$ (forced by the $d_k$ recurrence), the two-element sub-magma $\{x, c_1\}$ has a forced multiplication table. Checking E677 at $(a, b) = (c_1, c_1)$ gives $\text{LHS} = c_1$ but $\text{RHS} = x$. Contradiction.

  • Period 3: Assuming orbit $\{x, c_1, c_2\}$, three steps of E677 applications derive: (i) $c_2 \diamond c_1 = c_1$, (ii) $L_{c_1}(c_2) = x$, (iii) $L_x(z) = L_x(c_1) = c_2$ for an element $z$ that must be external to the orbit, contradicting $L_x$ injectivity.

  1. Period 4 is impossible (Theorem 9.1).

Case analysis on $C = L_2(c_1)$ at $n = 5$ (the minimum size for a period-4 orbit plus one external element). All three cases lead to bijectivity contradictions within $\leq 4$ E677 applications. Extended by SAT (CaDiCaL) to $n \leq 9$.

  1. Single-point reduction (Theorem 3.1). For period $p \geq 5$, E255 at $x$ is equivalent to the single identity:
    cp−4⋄cp−4=cp−5c_{p-4} \diamond c_{p-4} = c_{p-5}cp−4​⋄cp−4​=cp−5​
    This uses the recurrence $d_{k+1} = L_{c_k}^{-1}(c_{k-1})$ where $d_k = c_k \diamond x$, together with the anchor values $d_0 = c_1$ and $d_1 = c_{p-2}$ (both provable from E677).

  2. Squaring endomorphism equivalence (Theorem 7.1). In any finite E677 magma, the following are equivalent:

  • (a) E255 holds
  • (b) $S$ is an endomorphism: $(a \diamond b)^2 = a^2 \diamond b^2$ for all $a, b$
  • (c) Intertwining: $S \circ L_a = L_{S(a)} \circ S$ for all $a$
  • (d) Fixed-point property: for every $z$, the map $L_z \circ S$ has a fixed point

The (a)⟺(b) equivalence is verified by SAT at $n = 5, 6, 7$ and confirmed empirically on 90+ distinct models (sizes 5–35, affine and non-affine, including quasigroups and non-quasigroups). The equivalence requires finiteness — in the free E677 magma, $S(a \diamond b)$ and $S(a) \diamond S(b)$ are syntactically distinct terms.

  1. The 496-element blueprint model is entirely idempotent (Proposition 5.1), so its non-bijective $R_x$ is irrelevant to the non-idempotent case.

The open problem, reformulated

Proving E677 $\models_\text{fin}$ E255 is now equivalent to:

Prove from E677 + finiteness that $(a \diamond b) \diamond (a \diamond b) = (a \diamond a) \diamond (b \diamond b)$ for all $a, b$.

This is the "abelian squares" property — squaring commutes with the binary operation. In group theory, $(ab)^2 = a^2 b^2$ for all $a, b$ characterizes abelian groups. The analogous question here is whether E677 + finiteness forces this property in magmas.

The reformulation replaces the original existential target (find a fixed point of $L_z \circ S$ for each $z$) with a universal algebraic identity, which may be more tractable via:

  • semigroup theory (the transformation semigroup $\langle L_a : a \in M \rangle$ under $S$-conjugation),
  • minimal criminal arguments (in a smallest counterexample, the "defect set" $\{(a,b) : S(a \diamond b) \neq S(a) \diamond S(b)\}$ must be non-empty),
  • universal algebra / variety theory (Birkhoff's theorem, HSP characterizations).

@Jihoon Hyun - your proof that $x \mapsto L_x$ is injective ($L_y = L_z \Rightarrow y = z$) is a clean result. In the paper's framework, this is closely related to the uniqueness of left-fixers: E677 forces that if $w \diamond z = z$ then $w = \theta(z)$. Your simplified argument via $(xx)x = (yx)y \Rightarrow x = y$ gives a more direct path to this. It would be useful to have this as a clause in SAT encodings. Note also that a complete algebraic proof that period 4 is impossible is now in the paper (Theorem 9.1), independent of the SAT verification.

Defect propagation (new result)

Define the defect set $D = \{(a,b) : S(a \diamond b) \neq S(a) \diamond S(b)\}$. The diagonal is always non-defective: $(a,a) \notin D$ since $S(a \diamond a) = S(S(a)) = S(a) \diamond S(a)$.

Theorem (Defect Propagation Rule). For any $x, y \in M$, let $q = y \diamond x$, $r = q \diamond y$, $s = L_y^{-1}(x)$ (the four products in the E677 chain). Then:

If $(y, x) \notin D$ and $(q, y) \notin D$ and $(x, r) \notin D$, then $(y, s) \notin D$.

Proof. E677 at $(x, y)$ gives $x = y \diamond s$ via chain $q, r, s$. E677 at $(x^2, y^2)$ independently gives $x^2 = y^2 \diamond s'$ via chain $q', r', s'$. The three non-defect assumptions propagate: (1) $q^2 = q'$, (2) $r^2 = r'$, (3) $s^2 = s'$. Then $x^2 = y^2 \diamond s' = y^2 \diamond s^2$, and since $x = y \diamond s$, we get $x^2 = (y \diamond s)^2 = y^2 \diamond s^2$, so $(y, s) \notin D$. ∎

Contrapositive: every defect pair $(y, L_y^{-1}(x)) \in D$ forces at least one of the three "inner" E677 pairs to also be defective. Defects cannot be isolated — they form self-sustaining cycles in the propagation graph.

Minimal criminal structure: In a smallest counterexample, every defect pair $(a,b) \in D$ generates all of $M$ (since any proper sub-magma would be a smaller E677 magma where $S$ is an endomorphism by minimality, but the defect witnesses lie in the sub-magma). So $M$ is 2-generated, $|M| \geq 12$.

The remaining gap: to close the proof, one would show that the non-defect set $N = M^2 \setminus D$ — which contains the diagonal and is closed under E677 chain propagation — must equal all of $M^2$. The first step would require establishing that $(a^2, a) \notin D$ and $(a, \theta(a)) \notin D$ for all $a$, which would allow the propagation rule to extend from the diagonal via E677 at $(a, a)$.

A perfect-matching reformulation of E255, and why "construct the fixer" can't close it

Building on Lemma 13.2 and Adam McKenna's $P_z = L_z\circ S$ picture, two small things: a clean reformulation, and an obstruction that I think pins down the ceiling several of us have been hitting (Jihoon's cancellation lemmas, my earlier Prover9 reductions).

Notation. $M$ finite, satisfying E677. As usual $L_y x = y\diamond x$ (a bijection), $S(x)=x\diamond x$, and $\theta(x)=(x\diamond x)\diamond x$ is the left-fixer candidate - so E255 is exactly $\theta(x)\diamond x = x$. McKenna's map is $P_z=L_z\circ S$, i.e. $P_z(x)=z\diamond(x\diamond x)$. I'll also write $C_z(x)=(z\diamond x)\diamond z$ (pseudo-conjugation by $z$). By Lemma 13.2, E255 $\iff$ every $P_z$ has a fixed point, and $C_z$ has the same fixed points as $P_z$:
z⋄(x⋄x)=x    ⟺    x⋄x=Lz−1(x)=x⋄((z⋄x)⋄z)    ⟺    (z⋄x)⋄z=x.z\diamond(x\diamond x)=x \;\iff\; x\diamond x = L_z^{-1}(x) = x\diamond((z\diamond x)\diamond z) \;\iff\; (z\diamond x)\diamond z = x.z⋄(x⋄x)=x⟺x⋄x=Lz−1​(x)=x⋄((z⋄x)⋄z)⟺(z⋄x)⋄z=x.

  1. The fixed-point relation is a perfect matching.
    Let $\rho = \{(z,x)\in M\times M : C_z(x)=x\}$, and define two quantities (this is the only new language):
    deg⁡L(z)=#{x:(z,x)∈ρ},deg⁡R(x)=#{z:(z,x)∈ρ}.\deg_L(z) = \#\{x : (z,x)\in\rho\}, \qquad \deg_R(x) = \#\{z : (z,x)\in\rho\}.degL​(z)=#{x:(z,x)∈ρ},degR​(x)=#{z:(z,x)∈ρ}.
    So $\deg_L(z)$ is the number of fixed points of $P_z$, and $\deg_R(x)$ is the number of $z$ that "conjugation-fix" $x$.
  • $\deg_L \le 1$ is known (left-fixer uniqueness, Lemma 13.2): every $P_z$ has at most one fixed point. Hence $|\rho|=\sum_z \deg_L(z)\le |M|$, and **E255 $\iff |\rho|=|M| \iff \deg_L\equiv 1$.
  • Computationally, $\deg_R\equiv 1$ on all 678 magmas in the database: every element is conjugation-fixed by exactly one $z$. So $\rho$ is a perfect matching** of $M$ with itself, and $z\mapsto(\text{its fixed point})$ is a bijection. This is not right-cancellativity in disguise — in the non-RC model 77/65, $R_{S(x)}$ is non-injective for all 66 non-idempotent $x$, yet still $\deg_R(x)=1$.
  • The uniqueness half, $\deg_R\le 1$ - if $(z\diamond x)\diamond z=x$ and $(w\diamond x)\diamond w=x$ then $z=w$ (call it conjugator uniqueness) - looks like a clean candidate lemma, the same flavour as Jihoon's $\,y\diamond x=x\diamond x \wedge y\diamond(x\diamond x)=x\diamond(x\diamond x)\Rightarrow x=y$.
  1. The obstruction: no uniform witness.
    Call a map $g:M\to M$ a uniform witness if $g(x)\diamond S(x)=x$ for all $x$ (equivalently $x$ is the fixed point of $P_{g(x)}$).

Proposition. If a uniform witness $g$ exists, then E255 holds.
Proof. The hypothesis says $\deg_R(x)\ge 1$ for every $x$, so $|\rho|=\sum_x\deg_R(x)\ge|M|$. With $\deg_L\le 1$ we get $|\rho|=\sum_z\deg_L(z)\le|M|$. Hence $|\rho|=|M|$, forcing $\deg_L\equiv 1$, i.e. E255. $\square$

So exhibiting any uniform fixer/conjugator formula is equivalent to proving E255 - it can't be a stepping stone. The natural candidate $g(x)=S(x)\diamond\theta(x)=(x\diamond x)\diamond\big((x\diamond x)\diamond x\big)$ satisfies $g(x)\diamond S(x)=x$ on every database model, but it is E255 reshuffled:

θ = S◇x ⟹ L_S⁻¹(θ) = x (θ = S◇x by definition)
E677(S,θ): S◇(θ◇(g◇S)) = θ ⟹ θ◇(g◇S) = L_S⁻¹(θ) = x (pure E677, no finiteness)
⟹ g◇S = L_θ⁻¹(x)
∴ g(x)◇S(x) = x ⟺ L_θ⁻¹(x) = x ⟺ θ◇x = x ≡ E255.

Takeaway. The uniqueness lemmas ($\deg_L\le1$; conjecturally $\deg_R\le1$; Jihoon's cancellations) are genuinely non-circular and provable - but uniqueness never yields existence, and by the Proposition every constructive "name the fixer" route is circular. So a proof of E255 must obtain existence non-constructively(induction, or a global count / contradiction). That is exactly what a fibering result would give - e.g. Bernhard's size-49-over-$(4x{+}y)\%7$ program: is E255 preserved by the fibration? is a non-constructive existence statement of precisely the required shape.

(Methodology, per Bruno: everything above is checked against the full database - no Mace4. The Proposition and the $C_z\!=\!P_z$ equivalence are proofs; $\deg_R\equiv1$ and the candidate identity are verified on all 678 models.)

Write $\rho = \{(z,x) : (z\diamond x)\diamond z = x\}$, and set $\deg_L(z) = \#\{x : (z,x)\in\rho\}$, $\deg_R(x) = \#\{z : (z,x)\in\rho\}$. (Via $(z\diamond x)\diamond z = x \iff z\diamond(x\diamond x) = x$, these count the fixedpoints of $P_z = L_z\circ S$.) The one theorem we have is

$\deg_L \le 1$ (left-fixer uniqueness, Lemma 13.2),

so $|\rho| = \sum_z \deg_L(z) \le |M|$, and E255 $\iff |\rho| = |M| \iff \deg_L\equiv 1$.

Now the two halves of "$\deg_R \equiv 1$":

Existence ($\deg_R(x)\ge 1$ for every $x$) already is E255. If every $x$ has a conjugator, then $|\rho| = \sum_x \deg_R(x) \ge |M|$, which together with $\deg_L\le 1$ forces $|\rho| = |M|$ — i.e. E255. So a proof of $\deg_R\equiv 1$ would be a proof of E255, not a step toward it; what we actually have is just the computational check on the 678 database models (all of which satisfy E255). That's why I stated it as verified, not proved.

Uniqueness ($\deg_R(x)\le 1$) is the non-circular part. It says (z⋄x)⋄z=x ∧ (w⋄x)⋄w=x ⟹ z=w,(z\diamond x)\diamond z = x \ \wedge\ (w\diamond x)\diamond w = x \ \Longrightarrow\ z = w,(z⋄x)⋄z=x ∧ (w⋄x)⋄w=x ⟹ z=w, equivalently $z\diamond(x\diamond x) = x \ \wedge\ w\diamond(x\diamond x) = x \Rightarrow z=w$

  • i.e. the equation $z\diamond(x\diamond x) = x$ has at most one solution $z$. This does not imply E255 (it only re-gives $|\rho|\le|M|$), it's the exact dual of the proven $\deg_L\le1$, and it's the same flavour as your cancellation lemmas. The subtlety: it is not plain right-cancellation - that fails (the 77-element model has $R_{x\diamond x}$ non-injective for all 66 non-idempotent $x$), yet $\deg_R\equiv1$ still holds there. So it's a genuinely restricted cancellation at the pair $(x\diamond x,\ x)$.

So: the perfect-matching claim $= $ existence $\wedge$ uniqueness $=$ E255 $\wedge$ (the cancellation lemma above).

I did take a run at the uniqueness half with Prover9. In the quasigroup case it's immediate 12 steps from E677 + full quasigroup (it is just right-cancellation), so it holds in all right-cancellative models. The content is entirely the non-right-cancellative case (77/65 etc.), where $R_{x\diamond x}$ is non-injective: there Prover9 does not prove it from E677 + left-QG (auto2, 300\,s, SEARCH FAILED), and Mace4 finds no finite counterexample. So $\deg_R\le1$ mirrors the whole problem - trivial for quasigroups, open for the twisted models.
For contrast, the dual $\deg_L\le1$ does prove from E677 + left-QG (24 steps).

If you can crack the non-RC case with Prover9 I'd love to see it - it's a genuine new lemma -but note it won't close E255 by itself; the existence side is the whole problem. (z3 is useless here: inconclusive even on the proven $\deg_L\le1$.)

    preserved by quotients, products, and - the part that seems not to have been used in the
    thread - subalgebras. So by Birkhoff's subdirect representation theorem: if the nontrivial
    congruences of a minimal counterexample $M$ intersected to the equality relation, $M$ would
    embed subdirectly into a product of strictly smaller E677 magmas, all satisfying E255 by
    minimality - forcing E255 on $M$. Hence $M$ is subdirectly irreducible (s.i.): it has a
    monolith $\mu$ - a unique minimal nontrivial congruence contained in every nontrivial

    E255 fails componentwise, so $M$ is not a direct product; and $M$ is non-RC since the failing

    $M \to M/\mu$ is affine in that lemma's sense. So everything reduces to:

Why: normality makes the cosets a congruence for any word ($w(xn,yn') \in w(x,y)N$).
Writing each letter's contribution, $w(xn,\,yn') = w(x,y)\cdot \prod_i n^{g_i} \cdot \prod_j (n')^{h_j}$
where $g_i, h_j$ are suffix-products depending only on the cosets $(xN,yN)$ - and since $N$
is abelian, $n \mapsto \prod_i n^{g_i}$ and $n'\mapsto \prod_j (n')^{h_j}$ are
endomorphisms of $N$. So the fiber operation has exactly the form
$a_{\bar x,\bar y}(n) + b_{\bar x,\bar y}(n') + c_{\bar x,\bar y}$ with
$a,b \in \mathrm{End}(N)$, which is Lemma 13.4's hypothesis. ∎

and of course nothing more, so $\mathcal C = $ solvable. Supersolvable would be the analogous

at every simple non-abelian order. So:

abelian-normal steps + Lemma 13.4), and solvability is the precise boundary at which the
word-model restriction stops being a restriction.

vanishing fraction of the polynomial clone, so finding nothing there says little - and
finding anything would have been finding a general model, not a "word-model" in any useful

TL;DR. Building on the subdirectly-irreducible / one-generated reduction and the
Bonatto-school displacement machinery discussed earlier in this stream: every
prime-order E677 magma is simple with primitive LMlt for free (no extra conjecture),
so the criminal question at prime order splits into a tame (affine-type LMlt) and a
wild (2-transitive non-solvable) branch. The tame branch reduces to a single statement
("the multiplier A is constant"), which I can prove under a degree bound and which is
SAT-true for p ≤ 13. The wild branch is the genuinely hard half, and I think it is the
Bonatto–Stanovský school's home turf - that's open call #2.

  1. Prime-degree reduction (settled)

For |M| = p prime:

  • (A) M is simple and LMlt(M) is primitive. Why for free: E677 magmas are connected
    left quasigroups (the E677 identity itself exhibits x ∈ LMlt·y), connected ⟹
    congruence-uniform (Bonatto–Fioravanti, arXiv:2004.05368, Lemma 2.3), and a congruence
    with equal classes on a prime number of points is Δ or ∇ - so M is simple. A transitive
    group of prime degree is primitive. (No BLOCK=CONG assumption is needed at prime order.)

  • (B) Burnside dichotomy. A transitive group of prime degree is either ≤ AGL(1,p)
    (tame) or 2-transitive non-solvable (wild). Tame means every L_x is affine:
    x◇y = A(x)·y + V(x) with A: M→𝔽ₚ*, V: M→𝔽ₚ (a "twisted-affine" magma). Wild means LMlt has
    socle on the CFSG prime-degree list: Aₚ, PSL(d,q) with p = (q^d−1)/(q−1), PSL(2,11) on 11,
    M₁₁ on 11, M₂₃ on 23.

  • (B′) Tame + A constant ⟹ E255. If A ≡ a is constant then L_x is determined by V(x), so
    V is injective by L-faithfulness (Ibrahim's lemma); then every column R_w(x) = a·w + V(x)
    is injective in x, i.e. M is right-cancellative - a quasigroup - and 677 + quasigroup ⊢ 255.

  • (C) A prime-order criminal must be either tame with non-constant multiplier, or wild and
    one-generated. By (A)/(B)/(B′) the only way to fail 255 at prime order is (i) a tame
    magma whose multiplier A is non-constant (this is precisely what "A-constancy" below
    forbids, conjecturally), or (ii) a wild magma - and by the sub-magma localization argument
    (failing element generates M) it must be one-generated. The wild example we have, the
    sunflower at n = 89 (the simple non-RC database model, socle A₈₉), is decisively
    non-one-generated: every ⟨x⟩ is a 9-element petal. So one-generatedness is exactly the
    hypothesis that must kill the wild branch.

*(Composite order folds into this: a composite criminal is subdirectly irreducible
(Birkhoff) and one-generated, with a monolith μ; Dis_μ abelian ⟺ the monolith step is affine
⟺ handled by linear extension, and the simple case is the prime/primitive base above. The
companion DB-survey post verifies every composite non-RC one-generated database model has an
affine monolith step.)*

  1. Tame branch - a partial theorem, and open call #1

In coordinates x◇y = A(x)y + V(x), E677 is equivalent to (writing p₁ = y◇x = A(y)x + V(y))

A(y)A(x)·A(p₁)·y + A(y)A(x)·V(p₁) + A(y)V(x) + V(y) = x for all x, y. (E)

Treat A, V as the interpolating polynomials over 𝔽ₚ. Then A(p₁) = A(A(y)x + V(y)) has
x-degree deg A with leading coefficient (lead A)·A(y)^{deg A}. Reading off the top power of x
in (E) (the RHS has x-degree 1):

Proposition. A tame prime-order E677 magma with deg(A) < p/2 and deg(V) < p/2 has A
constant - hence is right-cancellative and satisfies E255.

The top x-power's coefficient works out to a nonzero function of y in each case
(d_A > d_V, d_A < d_V, d_A = d_V), because A never vanishes on 𝔽ₚ; if that power does not
wrap mod x^p − x it has nothing to match on the RHS, contradiction. Known tame models have
deg A = 0, deg V = 1 - comfortably inside the bound, and the bound's shape is right
(constant A forces V affine).

Open call #1 - a clean, self-contained finite-field problem (plausibly a few days for the
right person). Remove the degree bound: show E677 forces A constant in the high-degree
regime max(deg A, deg V) ≥ p/2 as well - equivalently, tame ⟹ right-cancellative at prime
order. I have it by SAT for p ≤ 13, and a second identity (from "Identity-iii", giving a
multiplier-difference relation Δ that mixes A at x, L_yx, L_y²x) that should pin the wrapped
coefficients, but I haven't closed the wraparound. This is pure polynomial-method over 𝔽ₚ.
Happy to share the exact (E)/(Δ) identities and the SAT encoding.

  1. Wild branch - the obstruction, and open call #2

The natural plan - kill the wild branch by O'Nan–Scott / socle analysis of LMlt - hits a
wall I want to state precisely, because it says the group alone is not enough:

Sub-magmas are not LMlt-blocks. In the sunflower (LMlt primitive, hence no nontrivial
blocks) two elements of a 9-element petal generate all 89 points as an LMlt-block. So the
sub-magma lattice (which controls one-generatedness) is orthogonal to the block/congruence
lattice (which controls the permutation type). One-generatedness is invisible to LMlt -
and the obvious magma-native proxy, the self-period |L_x-orbit of x|, also fails to detect
it (the database 77-model is one-generated with self-period only 7, generating M via
cross-fiber products).

So no purely group-theoretic argument on LMlt can settle the wild branch; it needs an
invariant that sees ◇ directly. The closest templates are the Bonatto-school quandle/rack
socle methods (e.g. Bianco–Bonatto, connected quandles of prime-power order), but those lean
on self-distributivity (the L_x being automorphisms), and E677 is maximally
non-self-distributive - so they do not port as-is.

Open call #2 - the months / new-theory one, and I suspect your home turf,
@Marco Bonatto and the commutator-theory folks. Everything reduces to:

Can a finite simple one-generated E677 magma have non-affine (2-transitive) LMlt?

In your language: is there a finite connected, non-self-distributive left quasigroup
satisfying E677 that is one-generated with non-abelian displacement group Dis? We've pinned
down that Dis_μ abelian ⟺ the monolith step is affine, so a "no" closes the whole
problem. I'd love to know whether the connected-quandle socle arguments have a
non-self-distributive analogue here, or whether there's a structural reason they can't -
and more broadly, whether the admissible-subgroup / commutator framework has leverage on a
magma-native (not block-based) notion of one-generatedness.

  1. Why brute search keeps stalling (evidence)

Two points, both settled:

  • No counterexample exists in the database - all 1473 current models satisfy E255
    (see the companion survey post for the breakdown by size and construction).

  • Certificate growth is steep and consistent across two independent encodings. Pure
    E677 + ¬E255 is UNSAT at n = 7 in 135s and n = 8 in ~5h (CaDiCaL), with DRAT lemma counts
    4k → 2.5M from n = 5→7; the Tao-Conjecture-1 NEG search shows the same blow-up
    (n = 7: 133s, n = 8: 6757s). Consistent with E677ₙ ∧ ¬E255ₙ requiring superpolynomial
    refutations - brute SAT will not reach the interesting sizes, which matches the structural
    picture above.

*All reproducible; scripts/notes available on request. Corrections especially welcome on the
prime-degree claims and the "sub-magmas aren't blocks" framing.*

I'm starting to worry that E677 -> E255 due to all simple finite E677 magmas being essentially "linear" (weaker version, all simple magma having E255), and all extensions preserving the core E255 feature. I think this can be made a bit more precise in a way that resolving this question would get at the core of the actual relationship between E677 and E255.

In case I'm accidentally using some terminology in a non-standard way, I'll define things here (please correct me if there are better terms).
I'm considering general extensions of a base magma (M,⋄M)(M,\diamond_M)(M,⋄M​) with fiber magmas (F,⋄x,y)(F, \diamond_{x,y})(F,⋄x,y​) where the label (x,y)∈M2(x,y) \in M^2(x,y)∈M2. Then the extension is the magma (M×F,⋄)(M \times F, \diamond)(M×F,⋄), with the operation defined as (x,s)⋄(y,t)=(x⋄My,s⋄x,yt)(x,s) \diamond (y,t) = (x \diamond_M y, s \diamond_{x,y} t)(x,s)⋄(y,t)=(x⋄M​y,s⋄x,y​t).

By a simple E677 magma, I mean a magma satisfying E677 which cannot be written as an extension of a smaller magma.

To define essentially "linear" here, let me use the defining property of a medial magma: (x⋄y)⋄(u⋄v)=(x⋄u)⋄(y⋄v)(x \diamond y) \diamond (u \diamond v) = (x \diamond u) \diamond (y \diamond v)(x⋄y)⋄(u⋄v)=(x⋄u)⋄(y⋄v). While medial alone does not imply any of left/right-injective or left/right-surjective, the implication (E677 + medial -> bijective), and therefore (E677 + medial -> E255), is easily proven by prover9. By the Toyoda theorem, a medial quasigroup can be modeled as x⋄y=f(x)+g(y)+cx \diamond y = f(x) +g(y) + cx⋄y=f(x)+g(y)+c for some abelian group (A,+)(A, +)(A,+), where f,gf, gf,g are commuting automorphisms.

We already have counter-examples showing E677 + finite does not imply medial, but all the E677 finite-field linear models are medial magmas. And since we only need the addition to be abelian, we do not actually need a finite-field. I think all the other concepts of "linear" considered so far also fit in here (so I think even something exotic like a non-associative non-commutative semiring "linear" model using matrices and the octonion algebra should still satisfy this definition of "linear").

So the slightly refined hypothesis is: all simple finite E677 magmas are medial.
The weaker version is: all simple finite E677 magmas satisfy E255.
